steps.title: Sun
steps.instruction: Trace the sun in the middle.

note.text: The sun holds 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.
note.remember: The sun has almost all the mass.

note.text: All eight planets travel the same way around the sun, in nearly circular orbits in about the same flat plane.

steps.title: Inner planets
steps.instruction: Trace the four small planets on those orbits.

note.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the terrestrial planets: small, rocky worlds with solid surfaces.
In reality, the outer orbits are far more spread out than any drawing can show.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant planets of gas, liquid and ice, with no solid surface.

steps.title: Gravity
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow from Earth toward the sun.

note.text: The sun's gravity pulls on every planet, always toward the sun.

steps.title: Motion
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow showing which way Earth is moving.

note.text: Earth moves sideways. Gravity keeps bending its path from a straight line into an orbit.

steps.title: Name the planets
steps.instruction: Pick the name of each numbered planet, counting out from the sun.

mistakes.Venus: Venus is second from the sun. Count the orbits: this is the third, Earth.

mistakes.Saturn: Saturn is sixth. This is the fifth planet, the first giant: Jupiter.

steps.title: Gravity's role
steps.question: If the sun's gravity suddenly switched off, what would Earth do?

options.text: Fly off in a straight line, in the direction it was moving
options.feedback: Yes. Without a pull toward the sun to bend its path, Earth would keep going straight.
Falling inward needs a pull toward the sun: that's gravity. Without it, Earth goes straight.
Nothing would slow it down in space. It would keep moving in a straight line.
Gravity is what bends Earth's path into a circle. Without it, there's no orbit.

steps.title: Holding together
steps.question: What holds the solar system together?

options.text: Gravity, mostly from the massive sun
options.feedback: Right. Every object pulls on every other, and the sun, with 99.8% of the mass, pulls hardest.
Magnets don't hold planets in orbit. Gravity does.
Space between the planets is nearly empty. Gravity holds the system together.
Without gravity, the planets would fly off in straight lines.
